title: Simpson’s paradox
objectives: Watch a trend reverse when groups are combined
Find the hidden variable that drives the reversal
Explain the reversal with a weighted average

screens.prose: A hospital compares two treatments for the same illness. Every patient was either a mild case or a severe case. Here are the counts.
screens.question: Fill in each recovery rate as a decimal.

hints.text: A recovery rate is recovered over treated, within one group.
Mild cases on A: 95 of 100.

feedback.correct: A beats B in both groups.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide recovered by treated inside each cell.

byKey.r0c2: B treated 300 mild cases, and 270 recovered: 270/300.
byKey.r1c1: A treated 300 severe cases, and 180 recovered: 180/300.
byKey.r1c2: B treated 100 severe cases, and 50 recovered.

explain.text: A beats B among mild cases, 0.95 to 0.90, and among severe cases, 0.60 to 0.50. So A looks better whoever you are. Now we put the groups together.

screens.prose: Same hospital, same counts. The hospital’s annual report ignores severity and gives one recovery rate per treatment.
screens.question: Fill in the totals and the overall recovery rate for each treatment.

hints.text: Add the two groups for each treatment.
A: 95 + 180 recovered out of 100 + 300 treated.

feedback.correct: B wins overall, though A won in each group.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add recovered and treated across both groups, then divide.

explain.text: Overall, A cures 0.6875 of its patients and B cures 0.80. A wins inside every group yet loses overall. A trend that reverses when groups are combined is **Simpson’s paradox**.

screens.prose: Why does A lose overall? Keep every group rate fixed, and change only how A’s 400 patients split between mild and severe.

derive.caption: A treats {{round(w * 100)}}% severe cases: A overall {{fixed(0.95 * (1 - w) + 0.6 * w, 3)}}, B overall 0.800

screens.question: Slide A’s share of severe cases down. Where does A’s overall rate first beat B’s 0.80?

options.why: At 75% A’s overall is 0.6875, below B’s 0.80. Slide down.
At 50% A’s overall is 0.775, still below 0.80. Keep sliding.

options.text: Never: B is the better treatment
options.why: Slide to 25%: A’s overall is 0.8625. The mix alone moves the overall rate.

hints.text: Watch the A overall bar as you slide.
Try 45%, then 40%.
At 45% A’s overall is 0.7925. At 40% it is 0.81.

feedback.correct: A overtakes B once fewer than about 43% of its cases are severe.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide slowly and read the caption.

explain.text: A’s overall rate is a blend of 0.95 and 0.60, weighted by its mix of cases. At 75% severe it sinks to 0.6875; below about 43% severe it beats 0.80. The **hidden variable** is severity: it drives both who gets A and who recovers.

screens.prose: Back to the real mix: 75% of A’s patients were severe cases, but only 25% of B’s.
screens.question: Which fact explains the reversal?

options.text: A was given mostly severe cases, which recover less often on either treatment

options.why: Both treatments had exactly 400 patients. The split inside each 400 is what differs.

options.text: A works worse on mild cases
options.why: A beats B on mild cases, 0.95 to 0.90.

options.text: The overall rates were added up wrongly
options.why: 275 of 400 and 320 of 400 are correct. The paradox survives correct arithmetic.

hints.text: Compare the severe bars with the mild bars.
Severe cases recover less on both treatments.
A’s overall is dragged down because three quarters of its patients are severe cases.

feedback.correct: Severity decides both the treatment and the recovery.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at which treatment got the hard cases.

explain.text: Severe cases recover less whatever the treatment, and A got three times as many of them. So A’s overall rate is dragged towards 0.60 while B’s sits near 0.90. Comparing the overall rates compares the case mix as much as the treatments.

screens.prose: Edge case. Suppose B had treated the same mix as A, 100 mild and 300 severe cases, with the same group rates, 0.90 and 0.50.
screens.question: What would B’s overall recovery rate be?

hints.text: Weight each group rate by B’s new mix.
Now 25% of B’s patients are mild and 75% severe.

feedback.correct: With the same mix, A’s 0.6875 beats B’s 0.60.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight 0.90 by 0.25 and 0.50 by 0.75, then add.

byKey.old: That is B’s rate with its old mix, mostly mild cases. Use the new mix: 300 of B’s 400 cases are severe.
byKey.plain: You averaged 0.90 and 0.50 equally. The mix is 1 mild to 3 severe, so weight them 0.25 and 0.75.

explain.text: B’s overall becomes $0.25 \times 0.90 + 0.75 \times 0.50 = 0.60$, below A’s 0.6875. With the same weights, a treatment that wins in every group must win overall. The paradox needs the groups to be mixed differently.

screens.prose: You are a high-risk patient choosing between two hospitals. A league table shows Hospital X saves 86% of patients and Hospital Y 79%.
screens.question: Which hospital should you choose?

options.why: You compared overall rates without checking the mix. X treats mostly low-risk patients. For high-risk patients Y does better, 0.75 to 0.70.
The rates differ within each risk group. For high risk, Y saves 0.75 and X 0.70.

hints.text: Which row describes you?
Read the high-risk row only.
High risk: X saves 140 of 200 (0.70), Y saves 600 of 800 (0.75).

feedback.correct: Y does better for high-risk patients, and for low-risk patients too.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the hospitals within your own risk group.

byKey.x: You compared overall rates without checking the mix. X’s 86% is high because 80% of its patients are low risk. Within each risk group Y does better.

explain.text: Y beats X for low risk, 0.95 to 0.90, and for high risk, 0.75 to 0.70. X’s overall rate is higher only because it treats mostly low-risk patients. Risk, fixed before the choice, drives both the hospital chosen and survival, so compare within risk groups.

screens.prose: Why does the mix matter? For one treatment, let $n_m$ and $n_s$ be the mild and severe patients, $r_m$ and $r_s$ those who recover, and $n = n_m + n_s$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: Overall rate $= \dfrac{r_m + r_s}{n}$, all recoveries over all patients
$= \dfrac{n_m}{n} \cdot \dfrac{r_m}{n_m} + \dfrac{n_s}{n} \cdot \dfrac{r_s}{n_s}$, splitting the fraction and multiplying each part by 1
$= w_m p_m + w_s p_s$, with $w$ a group’s share of patients and $p$ its recovery rate

hints.text: Start from the overall rate exactly as you computed it.
The second line rewrites each part as a share times a rate.
Overall rate, split into two parts, name the weights and rates, then put in A’s and B’s numbers.

feedback.correct: The overall rate is a weighted average of the group rates.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from all recoveries over all patients, then split it.

byKey.weights: The weights and rates come from the split line, so the split comes first.
byKey.nums: The numbers go into the weighted form, so they come last.

explain.text: The overall rate is a weighted average of the group rates, and each treatment uses its own weights. A puts weight 0.75 on its worse group; B puts 0.75 on its better group. Different weights can reverse an order that holds in every group.

screens.prose: Two traders, one year. Trader A wins 14 of 20 trades in calm markets and 32 of 80 in volatile ones. Trader B wins 52 of 80 calm trades and 7 of 20 volatile ones.
screens.question: Fill in each overall win rate, then each win rate if both had traded a 50–50 mix of calm and volatile markets.

hints.text: Overall: add the wins and the trades. At a 50–50 mix: average the two regime rates.
A’s regime rates are 0.70 and 0.40; B’s are 0.65 and 0.35.

feedback.correct: A is the better trader in like-for-like markets.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find each regime’s win rate first, then combine.

explain.text: B’s record looks better, 0.59 to 0.46, only because B traded mostly in calm markets. At the same 50–50 mix A wins, 0.55 to 0.50, as it does within each regime. Before you allocate capital, compare traders at the same mix of conditions.

screens.prose: A brochure says Fund Q’s trades won more often than Fund P’s over two years. Here are the trade counts by year.
screens.question: What is the full picture?

options.text: P won more often in each year; Q looks better only because most of its trades fell in the easier year

options.why: You compared the pooled rates without checking the mix. P beat Q in 2024, 0.60 to 0.55, and in 2025, 0.45 to 0.40.

options.text: P is better overall as well
options.why: Pooled, Q wins 130 of 250 and P 120 of 250. P is better only year by year.

options.text: The two funds are the same
options.why: The year-by-year rates differ by five points each year.

hints.text: Work out each fund’s win rate in each year.
2024 was the easier year for both funds.

feedback.correct: P won more often in each year; the pooled rate reflects the mix.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the funds year by year before pooling.

explain.text: P beats Q in 2024, 0.60 to 0.55, and in 2025, 0.45 to 0.40. Q’s pooled 0.52 beats P’s 0.48 because 200 of Q’s trades fell in the easier year. The year is the hidden variable here.

ideas: A treatment can win in every group and still lose overall.
An overall rate is a weighted average of the group rates, weighted by each group’s share.
The paradox needs a hidden variable that changes both the mix and the outcome. With the same mix it cannot happen.

formula.name: Overall rate
formula.tex: p = w_1 p_1 + w_2 p_2, \quad w_i = \dfrac{n_i}{n}
formula.note: Two treatments with different weights can reverse an order that holds in every group.

summary.trap: Comparing overall rates without checking the mix of groups behind them. Split by a variable that affects both the choice and the outcome, never by one the choice itself changes.

quiz.prose: A strategy wins 140 of its 200 trades in quiet months and 240 of its 600 trades in busy months.
quiz.question: What is its overall win rate?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the wins and the trades across both kinds of month.

byKey.plain: You averaged 0.70 and 0.40 equally. Busy months hold three times as many trades, so they weigh three times as much.

quiz.prose: Two treatments are each given to 300 mild and 100 severe patients. Treatment C has the higher recovery rate in both groups.
quiz.question: What can you say about the overall recovery rates?

options.text: C’s overall rate must be higher

options.why: With the same mix, both overall rates use the same weights, so C’s lead in each group carries through.

options.text: C’s overall rate must be lower
options.why: A reversal needs different mixes. Here the mixes match.

feedback.correct: Same weights, so the order cannot reverse.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the two overall rates use the same weights.

explain.text: Both overall rates are $0.75\,p_\text{mild} + 0.25\,p_\text{severe}$. C’s $p$ is higher in each term, so its weighted sum is higher. Simpson’s paradox needs different mixes.

quiz.prose: A study finds that people who carry lighters get lung disease more often than people who do not.
quiz.question: What is the most likely hidden variable?

options.text: Smoking, which makes people carry lighters and causes lung disease

options.why: You read the link as cause and effect. A third factor can drive both.
That would not change who gets lung disease. Look for something that drives both.

feedback.correct: Smoking drives both the lighter and the disease.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a factor that drives both things at once.

explain.text: Smokers carry lighters and smokers get lung disease. Compare smokers with smokers and non-smokers with non-smokers, and the lighter link vanishes. That is conditioning on the hidden variable.

quiz.prose: A desk’s large trades win 55 of 100. Its small trades win 195 of 300. A rival desk wins 0.58 on large trades and 0.70 on small trades, with 300 large and 100 small trades.
quiz.question: Which desk has the higher overall win rate?

options.text: The rival desk, because it wins more in each size
options.why: The rival wins more in each size, but most of its trades are large ones, its weaker group. Overall it wins 244 of 400.
The first desk wins 250 of 400, the rival 244 of 400.

feedback.correct: The first desk wins overall though the rival wins in each size.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out each desk’s overall wins out of 400.

explain.text: First desk: $\tfrac{55 + 195}{400} = 0.625$. Rival: $0.75 \times 0.58 + 0.25 \times 0.70 = 0.61$. The rival wins in each size but trades mostly in its weaker group: Simpson’s paradox again.
